Ele disse que, se eleito, pretende manter uma administração pública enxuta e garantiu que, em um eventual mandato, vai promover um corte de gastos no estado.

"A proposta de corte de gastos é gestão. Isso eu fiz. Fiz no meu clube quando fui presidente e fiz na Prefeitura de Belo Horizonte. Corte de gastos é corte de gastos. É apagar a luz. Se tem muita lâmpada acesa, apaga. Se tem muita secretaria, diminui. Isso aí é beabá de administração pública, na minha opinião", afirmou.

Depois do compromisso na CDL, Kalil participou de uma sabatina na TV Integração, afiliada da Globo em Uberlândia. Na entrevista, que durou 30 minutos, ele destacou propostas do seu plano de governo, como garantir atenção para os cuidados com a saúde mental.

articles.title: Ricky Hatton’s luxury mansion, where the boxing legend was found dead in 2025, sold for £1.5m, £350K below original asking price; five-bedroom home featured pool, gym and Manchester City memorabilia
articles.summary: UK News: The luxury mansion belonging to late boxing legend Ricky Hatton has finally been sold for £1.5 million, £350,000 below its original asking price, acco.
articles.body: The luxury mansion belonging to late boxing legend Ricky Hatton has finally been sold for £1.5 million, £350,000 below its original asking price, according to Land Registry documents cited by the Daily Mail.The five-bedroom detached property in Gee Cross, Greater Manchester, was initially listed for £1.85 million. However, following Hatton’s death last September, the home was taken off the market before being relisted at a series of reduced prices. It was eventually sold earlier this year for £1.5 million.Mansion was taken off market after Ricky Hatton’s deathHatton, a former light-welterweight and welterweight world champion, was found dead at the property in September 2025, aged 46. His body was discovered in the games room by his manager Paul Speak.The house had reportedly been placed on the market for £1.85 million shortly before his death. Following the tragedy, the sale was paused before the property returned to the market at £1.75 million. The asking price was subsequently reduced to £1.65 million before the eventual £1.5 million sale.Despite the circumstances surrounding the property, the estate agent’s listing made no reference to Hatton’s death. Instead, it described the residence as a “landmark modern residence offering luxury, space and unrivalled lifestyle features”.Inside Ricky Hatton’s lavish homeBuilt in 2010, the six-bathroom property had been extensively personalised by Hatton and reflected several of his passions, particularly his love for Manchester City.The grounds reportedly featured a traditional telephone box as well as seats from the club’s former Maine Road stadium. The property also offered expansive landscaped gardens with views of the surrounding greenbelt.Among its luxury amenities were a heated indoor swimming pool and jacuzzi, a private gym, cinema room and games room with a bar. A glass wall in the games area overlooked the pool.The principal bedroom suite featured a dressing room or walk-in closet, a deluxe en-suite bathroom, a crushed velvet chaise longue and dark patterned wallpaper.The mansion also included multiple reception rooms, open-plan living areas and a high-specification dark-panelled kitchen. CCTV and intercom access provided additional security.The estate agent described it as a “rare opportunity to acquire a truly outstanding home” in one of the North West’s most sought-after residential areas.Sale comes amid questions over Ricky Hatton’s estateThe property sale comes amid reports of uncertainty surrounding Hatton’s wider fortune. In July, reports claimed that disagreements had emerged over his estimated £40 million estate, with some members of his close family reportedly unclear about how his wealth would ultimately be distributed.Hatton, widely known by his nickname “The Hitman”, retired from boxing in 2012 after a celebrated career that saw him become a two-weight world champion and one of Britain’s most recognisable fighters.His death at the age of 46 sent shockwaves through the boxing world, with tributes pouring in from fighters, trainers and fans around the globe.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Ghepan glacial lake triggers disaster readiness drive in Lahaul Spiti
articles.summary: Lahaul Spiti boosts GLOF preparedness as Ghepan glacial lake grows 178%; HFL markings at 32 sites, early warning system planned, GSI study underway.
articles.body: KULLU: Within days of the devastating Nepal floods, Lahaul Spiti administration has stepped up preparedness against a possible glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) risk, and begun ‘highest flood level’ (HFL) markings at 32 vulnerable locations along the likely flood path of Ghepan lake, considering its expansion from 36.5 hectares to 101.3 hectares in just 13 years.Thirty-two residential areas from Sissu to the Sansari border have been identified and 128 locations are being marked as potential flood-prone zones.Ghepan Lake, located at an altitude of 4,070 metres, expanded by 178% between 1989 and 2022. Above Sissu and around 11km from the town, the potential downstream flood path extends for about 90 km through Udaipur to the district boundary.ISRO had informed the district administration in Nov 2023 that the lake had expanded considerably from its normal size and advised authorities to take necessary precautions, said Kiran Bhadana, Lahaul-Spiti deputy commissioner and chairperson of the District Disaster Management Authority.The HFL marking is being carried out under National Disaster Management Authority to create clear and permanent reference points indicating potential flood levels and to increase awareness among people living in vulnerable areas, Bhadana said.An early warning system (EWS) will be installed at Ghepan Lake this month through Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC), Thiruvananthapuram, to continuously monitor the lake’s water level and other critical parameters and provide timely information. The system was successfully tested at Sissu Lake in April this year.Ghepan glacial lake is 2,464 metres long and 625m at its widest near the glacial snout that gradually narrows towards the outlet. It is estimated to carry a volume of over 35 million cubic metres.A five-member team from Geological Survey of India (GSI) is scheduled to visit Ghepan Lake area for 14-day study during which they will assess the lake and its surroundings, measure lake depth and water flow, study meteorological parameters and examine areas vulnerable to avalanches and landslides. The administration will send a separate team to the lake this month to directly assess its current condition, said an official.As part of preparedness measures, rapid response teams have been formed in Sissu and Shashin villages, while residents in vulnerable areas are being trained and sensitised on disaster preparedness, rapid response and necessary precautions.The administration is constituting a district-level GLOF Monitoring Committee comprising officials from various departments, experienced mountaineers and other people with relevant expertise. The committee will conduct periodic field inspections and assess risks such as loose rocks, unstable terrain and other potential hazards, added the official.The number of glacial lakes in Himachal Pradesh has increased substantially in recent decades. articles.body: An Indian chemical company executive has been sentenced to 54 months in a US federal prison in what the US Department of Justice called the first-of-its-kind case as Bhavesh Lathiya is not an American, he does not operate in America; his company is in Surat. But Lathita, the founder and leader of Surat-based Raxuter Chemicals, pleaded guilty in April to smuggling and distributing fentanyl precursor chemicals.He was sentenced on September 2 by US District Judge Pamela K Chen in federal court in Brooklyn. Lathiya was also ordered to forfeit $24,560 and will be deported after completing his prison sentence, the US Department of Justice said. Prosecutors said Lathiya and his company illegally sold and shipped more than 50 pounds of chemicals used in fentanyl production to customers in the US and Mexico. The chemicals included materials capable of supplying all the ingredients needed to manufacture fentanyl through commonly used production routes.Packages disguised as Vitamin C and antacidAccording to court filings, Lathiya used deceptive shipping practices to evade customs and law-enforcement scrutiny. Packages containing controlled precursor chemicals were allegedly given false descriptions and accompanied by falsified customs documents.In one case, a shipment from Raxuter Chemicals that arrived in New York on June 29, 2024, was declared to contain Vitamin C. Investigators said it actually contained 1-boc-4-piperidone, a regulated chemical used in fentanyl synthesis.An undercover agent spoke to Lathiya demanding more supplyThe investigation later brought Lathiya into direct contact with an undercover US Homeland Security Investigations officer.During video calls in October 2024, the undercover officer told Lathiya that customers in Mexico were pleased with the quality of chemicals previously supplied and with the amount of final product they had obtained.Lathiya allegedly agreed to supply another 20 kilograms of 1-boc-4-piperidone. He also proposed disguising the chemical as an antacid.The shipment was eventually sent to the US in November 2024, with the package labelled as an antacid, prosecutors said.‘Source of the fentanyl supply chain’US officials portrayed the case as significant because it targeted the supply of fentanyl before the drug itself was manufactured. “During a national crisis when hundreds of Americans were dying every day of fentanyl overdoses, Lathiya smuggled and distributed chemical ingredients, including those that were the building blocks for this deadly drug, without any regard for the harm that his conduct would cause,” US Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr said.“With today’s sentence, the message is loud and clear that our Office will hold precursor traffickers like the defendant accountable for their role in the fentanyl supply chain.”Homeland Security Investigations Acting Special Agent in Charge Pete Gizas said Lathiya's activities placed him “at the source of the fentanyl supply chain”.“By feeding the market for fentanyl at its earliest stage, he turned chemical commerce into a direct threat to public safety,” Gizas said.The case was prosecuted in New York, but its alleged supply chain stretched across international borders, with chemicals originating from India and destined for markets including the US and Mexico.Lathiya was arrested in New York City in January 2025.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Markiplier GoPro trading claims: What the YouTuber said after $285M merger sent stock soaring
articles.summary: US Streamers News: YouTube star and filmmaker Mark “Markiplier” Fischbach has responded to speculation that he knew about GoPro’s upcoming merger before building an 8.5%.
articles.body: YouTube star and filmmaker Mark “Markiplier” Fischbach has responded to speculation that he knew about GoPro’s upcoming merger before building an 8.5% stake in the company. Markiplier became GoPro’s largest individual shareholder after accumulating 13.5 million Class A shares. The disclosure came shortly before GoPro announced a $285 million merger with Starman Optical. GoPro’s stock then surged, making the timing of Markiplier’s investment a major talking point online. Markiplier has denied having any inside information and said he had been buying the stock for months because he genuinely believed in GoPro’s cameras.Markiplier denies knowing about GoPro mergerThe timing of the events led some people online to question whether Markiplier knew about the deal before it was announced. Several posts on X speculated that his investment could have been connected to inside information.Markiplier addressed those claims during a YouTube livestream. He acknowledged why some people might interpret the situation that way but firmly denied knowing about the merger.“('Insider trading confirmed,' said a viewer) Uh no, I have to say that straight up. I know, but again, I see how it could be interpreted that way.”He also clarified that he did not suddenly buy GoPro stock after news of his investment became public.“I did not buy it on Sunday. I did not buy anything on Sunday. I had started collecting stock months ago, right? Months ago.”Markiplier said the ownership filing had already been submitted on August 20. He added that the process had started on July 23.“Even the filing, the filing which is required by the SEC for public ownership, I filed that, or it was filed, August 20, which you can find on GoPro’s website. I started that process July 23, right? It just took a long time to get there.”The filing shows that Markiplier held about 8.5% of GoPro’s Class A shares. The stake made him the company’s largest individual shareholder.Markiplier also said the merger itself was news to him. He claimed he did not know he had become the largest shareholder until the information appeared publicly.“I knew that I owned a good amount. I did not know that I was the single largest shareholder. So, when that article came out, that was news to me.”Why Markiplier invested in GoProMarkiplier’s investment was closely connected to his interest in GoPro’s cameras. He recently reviewed the company’s Mission 1 ILS camera and compared it with a much more expensive RED camera.In the review, he praised the GoPro while highlighting its much lower price.“The GoPro Mission looks amazing. You can see the speed difference between them if slow motion is what you need. This at one-tenth the price is kicking the RED camera’s a**. Sometimes this footage looks better. I’m not blowing smoke. I’m not paid to say that.”The review included a paid promotion notice and an affiliate purchasing link, but his 8.5% ownership was not disclosed in that video. That omission became another part of the discussion surrounding his investment.GoPro announced its Starman Optical merger on September 1. Under the deal, GoPro shareholders will receive a combined $285 million in cash, or $1.14 per share, while existing shareholders will retain around 10% of the combined company. GoPro also plans to expand into AI infrastructure, government, defense, robotics and aerospace while continuing to support its existing consumer products.Markiplier said the new direction was not what he had invested in.“If [GoPro] pivots away from making cameras, I’m not gonna be on board with that because, again, the only reason I invested in the first place was for the cameras.”He also said he was “genuinely sad” about the merger because he wanted GoPro to succeed through its camera business.“I wasn’t lying about anything I said in the video because the camera is legitimately good. I don’t know where it’s going. I don’t know what’s going to happen with it in the end. I think that it’s just sad. I’m genuinely sad because I really wanted GoPro to succeed because this is such a fun, cool little camera that can do so much.”Markiplier said he plans to vote against the merger, although he admitted his voting power is limited.“I’m going to take my tiny voting share, which is about 0.5%, I think, of the voting control of GoPro, and I’m going to vote against the merger, but it’s not going to do anything.”As of his livestream, Markiplier said he had not sold his GoPro shares. He also stressed that he did not make the investment with the intention of making money from a sudden stock surge.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Cleveland police chief proud of force but being 'let down' by funding
articles.summary: Victoria Fuller tells the BBC Cleveland Police needs to become part of a larger, strategic force with greater resources.
articles.body:
Cleveland Police's Chief Constable has said she is proud of her "brave" force but that it was being "let down" by the way it was funded, following a fatal crash which killed seven people including two police officers.

In her first sit-down interview since the A66 crash, speaking exclusively to the BBC, Victoria Fuller said the force needed to become part of a larger force with greater resources.

She said her officers are dealing with some of the highest crime levels in the country akin to those faced by metropolitan forces, but with less than half the number of officers.

Multiple people have since been arrested as part of a wider police operation against organised crime following the crash.

A Volkswagen Passat carrying five young men drove the wrong way down the motorway near Middlesbrough in the early hours of the morning before colliding with a marked police car.

Officers had been pursuing the car for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when the Passat turned on to the dual carriageway, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said.

Fuller, whose force covers an area of north-east England that includes Middlesbrough and Teesside, recalled being asleep when the duty commander rang her with the news.

"No matter how tragic and devastated you feel, we swing into action and we do what we need to do," she said.

The home secretary announced this week that Cleveland Police would be given an extra £2m to deal with the fallout from the crash, with 200 officers drafted in from elsewhere.

Fuller told the BBC on Friday that she was grateful for the support the force had been given, but added: "I need that all the time."

Cleveland's Labour police and crime commissioner has previously said the force needed an extra £20m a year to hire more officers and crack down on organised crime.

Cleveland Police is grappling with the highest recorded crime rate of anywhere in England and Wales, Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures for the year to March show.

At the same time, Fuller said Cleveland Police had experienced the largest decrease in the number of officers since 2010 and was staffed as if it were a rural force.

"It absolutely needs to change," she said.

Fuller expressed hope that reform to policing across the country was on the horizon, and that Cleveland Police would become one of the "big, strategic forces that have the resource, the flex and the capability to surge when they need to surge".

She added: "In the meantime, we need additional funding... to take us to that point."

Fuller denied that gangs had control over parts of Middlesbrough, describing it as a "complex" area to police, with high rates of school absence, drug addiction and mental health issues.

"We're doing the very, very best with what we've got - and we absolutely do need more."

Authorities say high deprivation and unemployment in the area are fueling organised crime.

"When young people have little aspiration or hope, who don't have confidence in the state, then unfortunately criminals exploit these people," Fuller said.

"They give confidence, and they give them hope, and they give them aspiration. And sadly what that means is young people doing things without thought of consequences."

The five who died in the Volkswagen on 22 August were aged between 17 and 23. Four of them had previous convictions, including for assaulting police officers and theft, Cleveland Police previously said.

Since the crash, the force has responded to at least two incidents it believes are in retaliation for the crash.

It has also had to grapple with a house fire in Middlesbrough that killed a woman and her niece, and left several others injured, which police could not rule out was linked to organised crime.

A 23-year-old man has been charged with murder in relation to the deaths of Natalie McDonald, 34, and Valentina Foster, seven.

Fuller also paid tribute to the two officers who died in the A66 crash - PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough.

"My heart goes out to their families - it really does," she said. "My grief can't compare to theirs, nor to the officers and staff who've worked closely with Matty and Tom for a long time."

The Home Office said it was grateful to Cleveland Police for delivering a robust response in difficult circumstances.

A spokesperson said: "We have been in regular contact with Cleveland Police and local leaders, ensuring they have the support they need and engaging on their financial concerns.

"This additional £2m targeted funding will help Cleveland Police tackle serious crime. Beyond this, the force will receive up to £197.8m in funding in the 2026/2027 financial year - a 3.7% uplift in cash.

"We have also committed to a wider review of the police funding formula to ensure that force funding is fair and responsive to local needs."

articles.title: Coal stock at thermal plants plummets, 'critical' at 50 units
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Coal stocks at thermal power plants across the country have fallen to less than half the recommended level, with 50 plants classified as ha.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Coal stocks at thermal power plants across the country have fallen to less than half the recommended level, with 50 plants classified as having 'critically low' inventories as on Sept 2 amid high electricity demand and monsoon-led disruptions in supplies, Central Electricity Authority data showed.The plants, with a combined capacity of around 224 GW, had 28.2 million tonnes (MT) of coal as of Wednesday, 48% of the prescribed requirement of 58.7 MT. The available stock is equivalent to about nine days of coal requirement at 85% plant load factor, against the normal requirement of around 19 days.The plants classified as short on coal stocks have less than 25% of their normative inventories. Coal ministry officials, however, said all critical plants were being monitored by an inter-ministerial team of officials on a day-to-day basis and regular fuel supplies were being provided to them.Of the 50 plants, 45 are based on domestic fuel, four are designed for imported coal and one runs on washery rejects.A senior coal ministry official said, "Classification of a thermal power plant as critical is a routine monitoring parameter under norms laid down by CEA. It simply means closer tracking and priority action. These plants are not running out of supply."Though the normative coal requirement at power plants is calculated at 3.1 MT every day at 85% plant load factor, officials said the actual requirement is around 2.4 MT.The monsoon sees supply disruptions every year. The situation starts improving from Sept onwards as rains begin to recede.While the power ministry did not respond to requests for a reaction, sources said some coal-fired plants had been asked to defer scheduled maintenance to ensure continuity of electricity generation.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Europe waking up to Modi's warning 'a bit late': Belgian PM
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI/MUMBAI: Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever on Friday said Europe had been slow to recognise the risks of becoming too dependent on other e.
articles.body: NEW DELHI/MUMBAI: Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever on Friday said Europe had been slow to recognise the risks of becoming too dependent on other economies, admitting that Indian PM Narendra Modi had warned it about the problem much earlier but was not heard.De Wever, who was on a two-day visit to India to strengthen ties in trade, investment, technology and strategic cooperation, said India and Europe were now facing similar challenges as economic dependencies were increasingly being used as leverage. "We do not like dependencies becoming weaponised against us. You have lived this history. Your Prime Minister warned Europe about this long time ago already. But he was ignored. He wasn't listened to. We are listening now," De Wever said at a Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) event.Calling Europe's awakening "a bit late", De Wever said the region was now having the "right debates" about who it could work with in a world where major economic powers were moving in different directions.He said India was the most important partner for Europe among countries that believed in multilateralism and cooperation based on "respect and not force". "If India is not on the list, then you have missed something fundamental. India is on that list. It's number one," De Wever said.In an apparent reference to China, De Wever said Europe was seeking to reduce its dependence on "big economical powerhouses" that were moving away from rules-based cooperation. "I will not name them China," he said, adding that such a direction was not what Europe wanted.Speaking on the occasion, Union commerce minister Piyush Goyal said the India-EU FTA was a win-win for everyone. "It will open opportunities for farmers, start ups, women entrepreneurs, it has something for everyone. It's been deftly negotiated protecting sensitive sectors on both sides. It offers huge potential for both sides," he said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'Exceptionally rare': All 3 hydraulic systems of plane failed together
articles.summary: India News: MUMBAI: Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau's preliminary report has confirmed what pilots and engineers call an exceptionally rare event, the near.
articles.body: MUMBAI: Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau's preliminary report has confirmed what pilots and engineers call an exceptionally rare event, the near-simultaneous loss of all three hydraulic systems on the A320neo aircraft at 36,000 feet. Hydraulic systems are the fluid-pressure circuits that physically move an aircraft's wing and tail surfaces. The green, blue and yellow systems dropped out within seconds of each other, triggering an autopilot disengagement, a stall warning and a brief altitude upset that injured 24 flyers.The accident occurred when the eight-year-old A320neo (VT-EXO) carrying 145 people had just been cleared to climb from 34,000 feet to 36,000 feet after entering the airspace controlled by Kolkata ATC. At 9:32:43am IST, within four seconds the flight control system detected loss of all the three hydraulic systems.‘Triple hydraulic failure close to unthinkable’In the next few seconds, the autopilot disengaged, a continuous repetitive chime sounded, and the stall warning triggered for two seconds. “The aircraft encountered altitude upset. Initially, it gained 372 ft and fell by 292 ft from its assigned 36,000 feet flight level during the event,” the report said.It did not give information on the cause of the triple hydraulic failure, nor did it put forth any safety recommendations for the A320 aircraft type. It said the investigation is in progress and hydraulic components, fluid samples and recorder data have been collected and are still being analysed.The critical information on the probable cause and contributory factors is likely to be released in the final report, expected to be published on or before Aug 4, 2027.In simple terms, hydraulic pressure is what physically moves an aircraft’s control surfaces, the ailerons on the wings that make it roll, the elevators on the tail that make it pitch up or down, and the rudder that makes it yaw left or right. Pilots move the stick and pedals, but it is hydraulic power that pushes the actual surfaces. An A320 carries three independent hydraulic circuits so that losing one, or even two, still leaves enough pressure to fly and manoeuvre the aircraft normally.“Losing all three at once is considered close to unthinkable, because the A320 has a triple-redundant hydraulic design which ensures no combination of failures can disable flight controls entirely. It is the kind of failure engineers cite alongside a handful of decades-old incidents involving other aircraft types, none of them an A320,” said a senior aircraft maintenance engineer. The notable total hydraulic loss events that occurred globally are the 1985 JAL 123 (Boeing 747), the 1989 United Airlines DC-10, and a DHL A300 that was hit by a missile over Baghdad in 2003.Following the triple hydraulic failure, the co-pilot, who was flying the aircraft, responded first to the upset before the captain took over the controls. Recovery was swift, the blue system came back within seconds, followed shortly by yellow and green, restoring normal flight control surfaces, the report said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Costa Rican president signals openness to domestic US military operations
articles.summary: President Laura Fernandez notes that Congress would need to approve any US military operations within the country.
articles.body:
Costa Rican President Laura Fernandez has suggested that United States military operations in the country’s territory could bring national security benefits.

But she added caveats. In an interview published on Friday, Fernandez emphasised to the news service Reuters that such measures would require approval from the national legislature.

She also added there were no plans in the works for US forces to operate in the country.

“It would obviously be very good for national security if it were about pursuing a common objective against transnational crime, transnational drug trafficking, transnational terrorism,” said Fernandez, a right-wing populist who took office in May.

Fernandez succeeded her mentor, former President Rodrigo Chaves , after a February election in which concerns about security and rising violence in the Central American country played a prominent role.

Though she ran on a tough-on-crime platform, Fernandez has said that she is not currently considering a state of emergency to address the problem.

Such emergency declarations typically suspend key constitutional rights, in favour of giving police or the military added powers to crack down on violence.

That model has been popularised under the right-wing president of El Salvador, Nayib Bukele .

But critics point out that the states of emergency are meant to be short-term measures, not permanent ones. El Salvador has been under an emergency declaration since 2022, with the government extending it dozens of times.

Crime has become a top voter concern in Costa Rica. The Central American country’s homicide rate has doubled in the last decade, reaching 17.2 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023.

That figure still places the country’s average well below many others in the region, but the change, partly attributed to increased drug trafficking activity, has startled many residents.

Fernandez’s remarks also reflect growing pressure from the US to reduce crime across the Western Hemisphere.

Since returning to office for a second term, US President Donald Trump has pushed to expand his country’s influence across Latin America, notably through military engagements.

Earlier this year, he launched the “Shield of the Americas”, also known as the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (ACCC), to bring together right-wing leaders across the region to address drug trafficking.

Trump used the inaugural meeting to encourage Latin American governments to embrace a military-driven approach to crime, despite concerns about human rights.

He has also carried out and threatened military operations in sovereign countries, on the premise of combatting crime.

Some countries, such as Mexico, have baulked at the prospect of US military forces carrying out operations on their territory. Critics point to Washington’s long record of interventions and rights abuses in the region.

But other countries have been more receptive. US forces, for instance, have recently carried out military operations with the right-wing government of Ecuador, in an effort to lower crime rates.

Ecuador’s armed forces, however, have been accused of crimes such as torture and enforced disappearance, abuses that experts warn could be worsened by support from the US.

A July report from Human Rights Watch warns that the military collaboration between Ecuador and the US has already had dire consequences.

Ecuadorian fishermen have reported facing attacks at sea, and in one case, Ecuadorian soldiers allegedly detained and tortured four Colombian farm workers, using methods such as mock executions, beatings and electric shocks.

That incident reportedly took place during a raid near the border carried out with US support .

“The two countries’ security relationship is deepening at a moment when both governments have engaged in serious human rights violations fueled by their insistence on framing their confrontations with organised crime groups as a kind of war,” the report says.

Those raids come after Ecuadorian voters rejected a referendum last year that would have allowed foreign countries to set up military bases in the country.

articles.title: Israeli police kill Palestinian in Jerusalem as army blocks aid for Qusra
articles.summary: Israeli forces bar Israeli and Palestinian activists from delivering food and medicine to homes besieged by settlers.
articles.body:
Israeli police have killed a Palestinian man in Jerusalem and the Israeli army has blocked humanitarian assistance from reaching an occupied West Bank village besieged by settlers for weeks.

Officers opened fire on a 33-year-old Palestinian near Damascus gate in Jerusalem on Friday. Israeli police said its border guard “neutralised” the man, claiming he was attempting to stab one of them.

The Palestinian Wafa news agency identified the man as Ibrahim al-Hendi from East Jerusalem’s Beit Hanina neighbourhood. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

Following the incident, Israeli forces deployed around Damascus Gate and the surrounding area of Jerusalem’s Old City, Palestinian sources told Al Jazeera.

Separately, the Israeli army said that it arrested Palestinians in the town of Qabatiya in the West Bank, alleging they were “planning to carry out an attack” against Israelis and security forces.

Ten other Palestinians were arrested during a 48-hour Israeli army operation in Nablus in the West Bank. The Israeli army said it seized more than “30 weapon production machines used to manufacture weapons” during the operation.

Meanwhile, Israeli settlers and soldiers carried out attacks across the occupied West Bank on Friday, Wafa reported. Settlers stormed the Khirbet al-Hamra community in the northern Jordan Valley and assaulted one resident.

Israeli settlers, accompanied by soldiers, also attacked Khalet a-Nahlah in southern Bethlehem. Israeli forces also fired tear gas and concussion grenades at a crowd of Palestinians who gathered to resist the attacks.

As violence and harassment of Palestinians continues across the occupied territory, the Israeli army on Friday also prevented around 100 peace activists from delivering food and medicine to Palestinians who have been under siege in the town of Qusra for 28 days.

Since August 9, Israeli settlers have besieged three Palestinian homes in the northern occupied West Bank village, while the Israeli army has also prevented the families from entering or leaving them, claiming the area is a “closed military zone”.

“Day 28 of the blockade on Qusra. About 100 activists arrived to deliver supplies to the besieged families,” the Israeli Peace Now movement said in a post on X.

“The army blocked us at first, claiming Qusra was a ‘closed military zone.’ Then let us in but on the way back detained us for ‘violating a closed military zone’,” it added.

Qusra Mayor Abdel Azim Wadi also told the state-run Turkish Anadolu news agency that the Israeli army has been “preventing the delivery of basic necessities to three families trapped on Mount Ras al-Ain”.

US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee told Israeli public broadcaster Kan on Friday that settler violence against Palestinians is “damaging the image of Israel as a nation and a people, warning that Israel “needs all the friends it can get” and “doesn’t need more enemies”.

Around 750,000 Israeli settlers live in 156 illegal settlements and 360 settlement outposts in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and carry out attacks aimed at forcibly displacing Palestinians, according to Palestinian figures.

articles.title: One of the largest spiders in the world remains largely unstudied
articles.summary: Hidden in the rainforest canopy of Southeast Asia, one of the largest spiders on Earth has spent over a century confounding scientists who struggle to agree...
articles.body:
For decades, a spider from the rainforests of Southeast Asia has confounded both experts and enthusiasts. Its story spans mistaken identities, groundbreaking discoveries, and an imposing appearance that belies its elusive life.

The Malaysian tiger tarantula wasn't always known by its current name. First described in 1891 by Swedish arachnologist Tamerlan Thorell, it has gone by several scientific labels over the years. Two names, Cyriopagopus schioedtei and Cyriopagopus thorelli, were still in use until recent clarifications by researchers. Now, experts agree: all refer to the same striking species, officially named Omothymus schioedtei .

This species is native to the Malay Peninsula but ranges across much of Southeast Asia. Its allure isn't limited to the wild. Spider enthusiasts worldwide seek it out, raising it far beyond its natural home.

What sets Omothymus schioedtei apart isn't just taxonomy. Its leg span can reach an impressive 22 centimeters, about 8.7 inches, while its body remains a comparatively modest 4 centimeters. It stands among the largest spiders on Earth, vying for attention alongside the legendary Goliath birdeater at 28 centimeters or the giant huntsman spider, whose outstretched legs sometimes top 30 centimeters.

The nickname "earth tiger" comes from the spider's bold, dark stripes. Males grow into light beige or olive-green hues as they mature, in stark contrast to the dramatically dark and stripy females. This sexual dimorphism makes telling the sexes apart almost as striking as the spider itself.

While its size might conjure images of a ground-dweller, this tarantula spends its life in the rainforest canopy. Omothymus schioedtei is arboreal, darting through the trees of humid tropical forests with unexpected speed and a reputation for defensive instincts.

The young gravitate toward the safety of loose bark, while adults prefer old, mature trees. Sometimes, these spiders even take shelter on human-made structures such as bridges, blurring the line between jungle and civilization.

Despite its formidable size, the Malaysian tiger tarantula remains surprisingly mysterious. Much about its true ecology, daily habits, and defensive strategies waits to be uncovered. Every sighting raises new questions, how does its life among the trees shape its evolution? What hidden behaviors could transform our understanding of these rainforest giants?

For now, the world's gaze lingers, drawn by a spider whose secrets may reshape what we think we know, not just about size, but about the wild complexity woven through every branch of its leafy home.

articles.title: Cave art discovery suggests first humans in Ireland came from Wales
articles.summary: During the most recent Ice Age, researchers believe there was a "lost land bridge" between Wales and Ireland.
articles.body:
Researchers believe the first known humans to set foot on Ireland thousands of years ago were most likely from Wales, following the "exciting" discovery of ancient cave art.

During the most recent Ice Age, when much of the British Isles were beneath a vast continental glacier, the depleted sea levels opened a "lost land bridge" between modern-day Pembrokeshire and the south-east tip of Ireland, around Rosslare.

According to rock expert Dr George Nash, from Liverpool University, the opportunities presented by this pathway would have been too good for hunter gatherers to ignore.

Now, alongside an international team of experts, Nash has located eight cave sites in south-west Ireland featuring rock art dating back from at least 15,000 years ago, around 5,000 years before the previous oldest example of humans in Ireland.

Nash, who coordinated the Lost Land Bridge Project, said there would have been a forested and grassland plateau around 46 miles (76 km) coast-to-coast.

With summertime temperatures typically -10°C to -20°C, Nash said the pathway would have supported wild horses, mammoth, bison, reindeer and other large herbivores, which fed off the hardy sedges, mosses and lichens growing through the fertile, but near-frozen soil.

Nash said he had always believed - from what he had gleaned throughout his career about human movement during the period - that it was inconceivable that people would not have utilised the opportunity the pathway presented.

This led him to assemble his multi-disciplinary team of experts from University College Dublin and the University of Adelaide, along with academics from Dubai, Wales and Portugal.

"Up until now the earliest evidence archaeologists had found - through accidental discovery - was from around 10,500 years ago, but everyone - not just me - knew that simply couldn't have been correct.

"We just weren't looking hard enough, and not in the right places. The principle we worked on was 'absence of proof isn't proof of absence'."

He said advances in artificial intelligence (AI) had been a game-changer.

"With the help of caving specialist Shane Diffily and digital mapping consultant Darren Lee, we were able to fill a computer algorithm with everything we knew about the characteristics of cave dwellings in south Wales and set it to work searching for similar sites in Ireland, without us trudging blindly around the countryside, hoping to bump into something which looked promising."

What their computer model spat out was 28 potential caves in south-west Ireland which the team investigated.

Eight of them were found to have cave art which they believe dates from at least 15,000 years ago and possibly much earlier, and around 5,000 years before the previous oldest example of humans in Ireland.

The team are currently unwilling to be more precise about the location of the caves, for fear that they may be vandalised or looted.

"We know that modern day south Wales was settled from around 35,000 to 40,000 years ago, by intrepid early modern humans from southern England, France and Spain, crossing the then dried-up land bridges of the English and Bristol Channels - seasonally settling in caves along the inhabitable strip of land stretching from Chepstow to St Davids," said Nash.

"Over 20,000 years their art progressed from primitive line drawings which may have been early tally charts, to more figurative and representative depictions of the world around them, and what we've found in Ireland is yet another progression from that."

The rock art which the Lost Land Bridge Project has uncovered includes engravings on the cave walls, paintings in ochre and charcoal and line sketches indented into clay and earth by fingertips.

Nash believes the growing population put pressure on humans to move ever more west and northwards.

"There were around 100 human-inhabited caves on The Gower Peninsula for example, in a time when the technology didn't yet exist for human groups to create their own free-standing dwellings.

"The ambient temperature within these caves would have remained between 10°C and 15°C all year round, so with bearskin covers and fires at the entrance - which also helped to ward-off predators - it would have been quite a cosy place to live, especially compared with the -20°C outside.

"Competition for these caves would have been intense.

"As family networks grew, knowledge of how to survive by following animal migration routes improved and they must have become bolder."

The Lost Land Bridge Project team believe the potential for more future discoveries is high.

"The sites we've currently explored are in south-west Ireland, but it's illogical to presume that early humans just bypassed Wexford, Waterford and Cork, and ploughed on west," said Nash.

"There must be more, and even earlier places which are just waiting for us to find them. This project is now pushing the boundaries of what we consider to be the final vestiges of a north-west European frontier. It's all very exciting."

articles.title: Nepal bet nearly everything on hydropower - the floods show why that's a problem
articles.summary: More than 10% of Nepal's energy generation capacity was knocked out by last week's floods.
articles.body:
Almost 100% of Nepal's electricity comes from hydropower, and it produces so much it earns nearly $200m (£147m) each year exporting hydroelectricity to India and Bangladesh.

But the very glaciers and mountains giving Nepal this massive natural advantage are succumbing to global warming - and last Wednesday's deadly floods have laid bare the risks to the nation's hydropower ambitions.

More than 1,300 people were killed, while thousands more are still missing.

The floods, which destroyed entire villages near the border of Nepal and Tibet, severely damaged 12 hydropower plants in the Trishuli River basin and knocked out more than 10% of Nepal's total power generation capacity. Operators tell the BBC they don't yet know if any of these facilities can be brought back to operation.

The state-owned Nepal Electricity Authority, which owns six of the 12 damaged facilities, has assured Nepalese households that supply remains adequate. But its spokesman Rajan Dhakal acknowledges that with climate-related disasters becoming more frequent, "the time has come for a rethink of our hydropower policy".

Only two-thirds of people in Nepal had access to electricity in 2010, and even connected households would face power cuts for up to 16 hours a day.

An expansion of hydropower infrastructure alongside efforts to tackle corruption and boost energy imports from India to fill seasonal gaps meant that by 2018, most of Nepal was enjoying 24 hours of power supply per day.

At present, there are 225 hydropower plants across Nepal with more than 3,900MW of installed capacity, according to the Nepal Electricity Authority - capable of powering some three million households simultaneously.

Hundreds more such facilities are either being constructed or in the pipeline. Most of them are built high up in the mountains, where they can seize fast-flowing currents to generate power. These projects require little to no storage system.

However, with the high-altitude regions of the Himalayas warming 50% faster than the global average, they face greater environmental risks. Preliminary investigations have pointed to a collapsed glacier and its bedrock as the cause of last week's flash flood.

While scientists say it is too soon to draw any firm links to climate change, Nepal's Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority previously said more than nine in 10 disaster events recorded between 2018 and 2024 were "related to climate".

Nepal's former Energy Minister Kulman Ghising, who called the catastrophic deluge a "once-in-a-century" event, says it holds lessons for designing plants and picking sites where they are built.

"We need to design the plants [to be more] resilient to the floods and, most importantly, adopt early-warning systems as well as robust emergency evacuation measures," he told environmental news outlet Mongabay.

Potentially hundreds of hydropower labourers, engineers and residents are thought to be trapped inside the mud-filled tunnels of these plants since the floods hit.

A "rethink" of Nepal's hydropower strategy could involve reservoir-based plants that need not be situated up in the mountains, says Dhakal from the Nepal Electricity Authority. These could allow water to be stored and released as needed, but would also involve significant economic and environmental costs.

Some question if Nepal has been too reliant on hydropower.

"We should not be putting all our eggs in one basket in these dangerous times," says renewable energy expert Kushal Gurung, who founded the clean tech firm WindPower Nepal.

"We need to seriously embrace other alternatives as well, like solar and wind. And for that we will need to revise our energy policy that is at the moment very pro-hydropower," he says.

The claim is echoed by Vivek Shastry, researcher at Columbia University's Center on Global Energy Policy, who argues that "meaningful additions of wind and solar generation is a resilience strategy that can limit single-point or interconnected electricity system failures in the future".

A report from the German aid agency suggests the technical potential for energy production from solar power in Nepal is around 10 times larger than that of hydropower.

Puspa Sharma, a senior research fellow at the National University of Singapore's Institute of South Asian Studies, agrees Nepal has to diversify its energy sources, but warns this can be done "only to a limited extent".

"While there is untapped capacity in wind and solar, hydropower really is the one that gives Nepal massive competitive advantage vis-a-vis its South Asian neighbours," he says, citing various studies comparing renewable energy potential in the region.

Hydropower continues to dominate large-scale investments in Nepal, and some climate activists say the funding has continued despite known disaster risks.

The Upper Trishuli-1 project, which has been all but destroyed after last week's floods, was one of Nepal's largest foreign direct investment ventures, valued at about $647m. Its backers include the Asian Development Bank and the International Finance Corporation.

The Upper Trishuli 3A, which has also been severely hit, was funded by China's Export-Import Bank.

Himanshu Thakkar, coordinator of the South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers & People, says international lenders were "acutely aware of the extreme danger to which they were exposing thousands of labourers, officials, residents, rivers, infrastructure and landscape".

"Their own reports repeatedly highlighted it. But they did not take any preventive steps, did not demand stringent checks and balances, nor were they prepared for a calamity they knew could occur," he says.

History has already shown the Trishuli River basin to be volatile, Thakkar says, pointing to how it had been hit by floods in the last two years. In September 2024, an unprecedented cloudburst over the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi river basins sparked flash floods in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading - settlements by the river that are also among the hardest hit from last week's floods.

Then in July 2025, a glacial lake in Tibet's Gyirong county burst and swept down this very same stretch of river into Nepal, killing at least 11 people. That flood damaged critical infrastructure and halted trade along the busy Nepal-China corridor. The border crossing was shut for nearly six months and had only reopened on 1 January this year.

Dhakal from the Nepal Electricity Authority admits that even if climate risk assessments were carried out correctly, "the designing of the plants may not have been done accordingly".

"Clearly we will need to improve in the way we build and operate our hydropower plants," he adds.

Private operators are already feeling the financial impact. Insurers have paid out around $40m for flood-related damage to more than 20 privately owned plants over the past three years, according to Uttam Bhlon Lama from the Independent Power Producers' Association of Nepal.

He warns insurance premiums are rising significantly and making the cost of doing business "unfeasible".

This disaster shows climate risks are international and cannot be managed by Nepal alone, suggests Manjeet Dhakal, a member of the country's climate delegation at the UN Climate Change Conference.

Governments and international organisations must share data, assess impacts and develop early-warning systems together, he urges.

"Nepal is among the least responsible for the greenhouse emissions that led to these exacerbated risks.

"Ironically, our hydropower industry is an attempt to reduce our already minimal emissions... We cannot, and should not, be made to respond to these risks alone."

articles.title: Offord pledges to scrap tax system and boost jobs under Reform
articles.summary: Reform UK's leader in Scotland will set out his priorities in a speech to the party conference later on Saturday.
articles.body:
Reform UK's leader in Scotland will promise to scrap the six-band income tax system, boost jobs and address immigration in his speech to the party's conference later.

Malcolm Offord is set to address members on the final day of the gathering in Birmingham.

Ahead of his speech, the West Scotland MSP said his party showed that "real world experience can top tired tropes from out-of-touch career politicians".

He claimed the SNP has "run Scotland aground" and urged voters to choose "Reform's fresh and decisive thinking".

"Things are looking very bleak for Scotland: the economy is stagnating and we are staring at a massive £5bn blackhole with no solutions forthcoming from the tired SNP government," he said.

"There are fewer jobs, the benefits bill is ballooning and households are struggling from higher taxes, leaving Scots with less money in their pockets."

Offord took aim at Scotland's six tax band system, which contrasts with the three bands in England, Wales and Northern Ireland.

"The six-band tax system needs to go, we must start listening to our business leaders to boost jobs and growth across the country and it's time to address the Scottish exceptionalism at the top of government that has allowed immigration to bankrupt Scottish councils."

Offord led Reform to a breakthrough in the Scottish Parliament elections in May, securing 17 MSPs to make them the joint second largest party in Holyrood.

His speech follows UK party leader Nigel Farage who addressed the conference on Friday in the wake of a Channel 4 News report about two men who apparently suggested a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations for the party.

The programme featured undercover filming by Verbatim Investigations

Farage's senior aide Dan Jukes and Reform's head of policy James Orr have both stood down pending the outcome of an internal probe

In his speech, Farage said his party has "broken no law" and referred to the filming as "entrapment".

Verbatim Investigations told the BBC its reporting was "carried out to the highest journalistic standards".

Describing Britain as "broken", Farage also used his speech to attack Prime Minister Andy Burnham for having "no mandate".

He outlined a series of policies, promising "radical" tax cuts and saying a Reform government would put a stop to small boat crossings in its first 100 days.

Meanwhile, he threatened to get rid of the House of Lords in a referendum if the upper chamber failed to pass Reform legislation, describing the party's attitude as "can do, will do".

articles.title: Africa bigger, US smaller - UN adopts new map
articles.summary: The United Nations General Assembly voted Friday to adopt a new world map that makes the African continent bigger while shrinking North America and Europe, d...
articles.body:
The United Nations General Assembly voted Friday to adopt a new world map that makes the African continent bigger while shrinking North America and Europe, drawing ire from Washington.

Aimed at "a more accurate representation" of continental landmasses, the resolution was supported by 164 countries while the United States voted against it and six other states abstained.

The new map -- known as the Equal Earth cartographic projection -- improves "the accuracy of the cartographic representation of the world," the resolution said.

It urges member states to use the new map in place of the traditional Mercator projection, which was designed for maritime navigation by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569.

Foreign Minister Robert Dussey of Togo, which sponsored the resolution, said maps "guide education, nourish the imagination, and influence collective perceptions."

"They are therefore never neutral; when they present a distorted image of our planet, they risk perpetuating inaccurate representation that is passed down through generations."

The United States however slammed the resolution, saying such moves are "the reason this institution is losing its credibility."

"Instead of focusing on genuine problems... this body is debating map projects from the 16th century and their role in promoting reparations and cognitive justice," US representative Yaryna Ferencevych said ahead of the vote.

The Mercator projection focused on accurate depictions of the shapes and angles of land masses, but their relative sizes were often inaccurate -- largely due to the challenge of rendering a three-dimensional globe onto a two-dimensional map.

It inflated northern regions and compressed equatorial ones, making Europe and North America appear much larger, while shrinking Africa and South America.

A group of cartographers launched the Equal Earth projection in 2018. It makes Africa, Latin America, South Asia and Oceania appear much larger.

"Equal Earth preserves the relative surface areas of continents and, as much as possible, shows their shapes as they appear on a globe," one of the cartographers, Bojan Savric, told AFP in 2025.

France -- which co-sponsored the resolution in support of the new map -- announced Friday that it would abandon the Mercator projection.

In that map, "the United States, Russia and China take on a disproportionate visual prominence compared to Africa, Latin America or southeast Asia," while "Greenland appears almost as big as Africa," Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said.

"Changing maps obviously doesn't change the world," he said. "But correcting a distorted representation is already an act of truth."

The initiative comes as France is seeking to improve relations with Africa, particularly in former colonies with which it has prickly ties.

articles.title: Viral Videos of Park Visitors Squatting and Posing on a Live Tortoise Spark Outrage
articles.summary: The incident occurred in an animal experience area at Changlu Tourism and Leisure Park in China
articles.body:
A viral video shows theme park visitors in China standing on a tortoise, sparking outrage and changes to the park's policies

Experts warn tortoise shells are living tissue and can sustain hidden injuries despite appearing unharmed

Similar incidents of animal mistreatment at parks and zoos have drawn public condemnation and legal consequences

A viral video showing theme park visitors standing on a live tortoise has sparked widespread outrage and prompted the park to crack down on animal mistreatment.

The footage, filmed in August at Changlu Tourism and Leisure Park in Guangdong Province, China, and obtained by Newsflare, shows a guest stepping onto a tortoise's back and squatting on the reptile while holding a child. The incident occurred in the park's designated animal-experience area, despite signage instructing visitors not to sit or stand on the animals.

In the clip, the tortoise appears to struggle under the added weight. Amid growing outrage over the video, the park said it would implement new blacklisting policies to prevent animal cruelty, according to Newsflare. The park told the outlet that a veterinarian examined the tortoise after the recorded incident and found it in good health.

While a shell may look like sturdy armor, experts note it is far more vulnerable than it appears. According to Spruce Pets , a tortoise's shell is living tissue fused to its skeleton, and pressure from being stepped on can cause severe fractures that aren't visible from the outside. That means an animal can appear unharmed while having sustained serious damage.

The incident is only the latest example of park and zoo visitors mishandling animals in ways that draw public condemnation.

In March 2025, a man was arrested after climbing into the enclosure of Moo Deng, the viral pygmy hippo, at the Khao Kheow Open Zoo in Thailand, as PEOPLE previously reported. Security footage showed the intruder taking photos before climbing back out. The zoo confirmed that Moo Deng and her mother, Jona, were unharmed, and police charged the man with trespassing.

Other cases have ended far more dangerously for the person involved. In April 2025, a 29-year-old man visiting a zoo in the Philippines climbed into a crocodile enclosure to pose for photos because he believed the animal was fake, PEOPLE previously reported.

The crocodile, a female named Lalay, bit down on his arm and dragged him through the shallow water as onlookers screamed. A zookeeper eventually struck the animal with a piece of concrete to free the man, who later received more than 50 stitches.

articles.title: Mysterious $150M superyacht docks in LA with hidden name and magical connection
articles.summary: Author J.K. Rowling's $150 million superyacht Samsara is reportedly docked in a Los Angeles marina with its name covered, but locals quickly identified the 290-foot vessel.
articles.body: A mysterious nine-figure superyacht sailed into a Los Angeles marina with its name concealed, but locals apparently didn't need long to figure out the famous name behind the massive vessel. The boat, which has been docked in Marina del Rey since Sunday, belongs to "Harry Potter" author J.K. Rowling, according to the California Post. The Post cited its sources, one of whom called it "the worst kept secret on the Marina." MASSIVE NEW CRUISE SHIP UNVEILS JAW-DROPPING OUTDOOR THEME PARK IN MIDDLE OF THE OCEAN The yacht's name was reportedly covered soon after docking, but that did little to keep the vessel's identity under wraps. The superyacht was spotted by those behind the Instagram account twogirls.oneboat, with several commenters identifying the vessel as Rowling's Samsara, according to the Post. The Post reported that while Rowling has been confirmed as the owner, the "Harry Potter" author has not been seen publicly. Pictures show the enormous white superyacht docked in the marina, towering over its surroundings. BELOVED CRUISE SPOT WILL BE OFF LIMITS THROUGH 2027 AS SAFETY CONCERNS LINGER Superyacht broker Chris Cecil-Wright told Fox News Digital owners will sometimes take steps to make their vessels less easily identifiable, although he said concealing a yacht's name is "very rare." "Quite often, you'll find that if a boat is at anchor or in a port you might switch off AIS [Automatic Identification System], so people can't instantly work out where you are," the United Kingdom-based expert said. "Very occasionally, if there's a particular event or something going on, you might find an owner might conceal the obvious names on the side of the boat." Cecil-Wright said privacy itself is a major draw for wealthy and high-profile yacht owners. "Particularly when you're a recognizable face or name, it becomes increasingly difficult to be able to relax anywhere in public," he said. CLEANEST CRUISE LINES REVEALED AFTER CDC SURPRISE SANITATION INSPECTIONS "So being on a private yacht, which is often sort of looked at as a private island, is the real luxury." At 290 feet long, the ship is nearly the length of a football field. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The vessel can accommodate 12 guests and a crew of 26, and features a circular swimming pool, cinema and beach club, according to the website SuperYachtFan. The superyacht was built by Oceanco and delivered in 2015 under the name Infinity. The yacht is worth an estimated $150 million, according to SuperYachtFan, with an estimated running cost of up to $15 million a year. The ship's first owner was businessman Eric Smidt, who sold it to Australian billionaire businessman Brett Blundy. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS In 2023, the ship was sold to Rowling, who named the boat Samsara, a Sanskrit word meaning "wandering." Fox News Digital reached out to Rowling, but she declined to comment. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Rowling, who was a single mother receiving government assistance when "Harry Potter" was published, has since become one of Britain's wealthiest authors. Her net worth stood at a staggering $1.2 billion as of Sept. 4, according to Forbes. For the ultra-wealthy, superyachts offer a rare combination of luxury and privacy, essentially serving as floating mansions that can travel from one exclusive destination to another. articles.title: Man arrested after alleged box cutter incident injures 16-year-old co-worker at restaurant, Palestine PD says
articles.summary: An Elkhart man was arrested after a suspected horseplay incident with a box cutter injured a 16-year-old co-worker at a Palestine Cotton Patch Café, the Pale...
articles.body:
An Elkhart man was arrested after a suspected horseplay incident with a box cutter injured a 16-year-old co-worker at a Palestine Cotton Patch Café, the Palestine Police Department said.

According to a post, Jose Buenrrostro, 47, allegedly attacked the co-worker with a "bladed instrument" on Sept. 2. The co-worker sustained a cut to his arm, and it was reported that Cotton Patch management told the teen to tend to his own wound with a medical kit in the restaurant and directed him to finish his shift waiting tables. Buenrrostro remained at work.

After the shift, the teen was taken by a parent to seek medical treatment for the injury and received two sutures.

The police department was made aware of the incident on Sept. 3, and detectives then began the investigation.

An arrest warrant was obtained on Sept. 4 for Buenrrostro, and he was arrested at his home.

The investigation is ongoing, and additional charges are possible.

articles.title: German president calls for unity in democracy ahead of landmark vote
articles.summary: German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on Friday called for the country's democracy and rule of law be protected from those "who scorn and trample all over...
articles.body:
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on Friday called for the country's democracy and rule of law be protected from those "who scorn and trample all over them," ahead of Sunday's state election that can bring the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) to power.

"Ethnic-based thinking and nationalist isolationism are simply not the answer to the challenges of the 21st century," Steinmeier told a community festival attended by 2,000 volunteers at his secondary residence in Bonn.

Steinmeier, who steps down from office in March after ten years, described liberal democracy as an "achievement" and "a blessing for us all."

It helps to realize that those who wish to protect and preserve democracy represent the majority, said Steinmeier.

The comments came two days before the AfD is expected to win enough votes in the election in the eastern federal state of Saxony-Anhalt to take control there.

Founded in 2013, the rapidly ascendant party embraces a hard Euro-sceptic, anti-immigration platform steeped in far-right rhetoric, and is defiant of frequent calls for it to be banned from German political life as being outright extremist.

Anger and outrage offer no way forward, continued Steinmeier, who made no mention of the party or election in his comments. "You cannot build a future on hatred and incitement."

Addressing the volunteers gathered at the historic Villa Hammerschmidt, the 70-year-old president said: "We need people like you right now, and you all need the support of the many in our country - the large, often too silent majority."

Under the title "At Home in Germany: How We Live Together," the subsequent panel discussion focused on living together in a "country with a migration background." articles.title: Germany's far-right AfD bids for first taste of power in eastern vote
articles.summary: If it wins an outright majority in Saxony-Anhalt, it would be the first time a far-right party has held state-level power in Germany since World War Two.
articles.body:
Germany is holding its breath this weekend as there is a seismic election in the country's east.

The Alternative für Deutschland party is aiming to secure a majority in the regional parliament of Saxony-Anhalt.

An outright win would mark the first time a far-right party has held state-level power in the nation's post-war era.

For the AfD's opponents, this is a point of serious peril. But the party sees it as a stepping stone towards its dreams of nationwide power.

This is an election that could change German history.

The result could also spell fresh trouble for embattled conservative (CDU) Chancellor Friedrich Merz, as rumours persist about whether he can see out his term in office.

Booed during recent public appearances, Merz is hardly seen as an electoral asset.

Perhaps the chancellor regrets a pledge to halt the rise of the far right, given that the exact opposite has happened.

By contrast, the charismatic AfD lead candidate in the state - Ulrich Siegmund - appears to have enjoyed dominating discussion and media coverage.

Dubbed "Germany's Most Dangerous Man" by Der Spiegel magazine, he has brushed off reports that people previously in the neo-Nazi scene are among those to hold influential roles around him.

The 35-year-old can often be seen, including in his own many social media posts, amongst adoring crowds or happily riding a retro East German scooter.

A lingering nostalgia for the past, alongside an acute dissatisfaction with the present, has fed the party's popularity in its eastern strongholds.

Voters voice frustration with immigration, public safety, Germany's struggling economy, high energy costs and aid being sent abroad to countries like Ukraine.

Some people I have spoken to passionately believe that the AfD is offering a real chance for radical change - and say Ulrich Siegmund has given them hope.

Other supporters are less certain, but say they have lost faith with mainstream parties that have dominated politics for decades.

An AfD lawmaker once told me that if they got a shot at regional government, then people would see the "sky won't fall in".

Some of the movement's detractors may disagree. Its plans, for Saxony-Anhalt, are highly controversial within Germany.

The party wants to segregate child refugees into special classes: "The refugee children should be given the message that their stay in Germany is only temporary."

The manifesto claims that "sexual deviations and non-reproductive lifestyles" have been aggressively promoted over "normal family" structures.

LGBT rainbow flags should be banned from being flown at schools, the party argues, while children should be taught less about the Nazis and more about positive aspects of German history.

On immigration, a task-force would be set up as part of plans to detain and deport migrants who no longer have the right to be in the state, while the party also calls for an end to "illegal, culturally alien" mass migration.

The AfD's pro-Russia sympathies have also sparked claims that it cannot be trusted with sensitive intelligence. When a Russian army mug was spotted in the office of leading AfD figure Hans-Thomas Tillschneider in Saxony-Anhalt, he said it was just a souvenir, and "it's not our war".

That was as Berlin, this week, publicly blamed Moscow for a failed drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport. The Kremlin has denied involvement.

Meanwhile, German security sources have warned that Russian-backed disinformation campaigns, often against AfD rivals, have been escalating - something Moscow's representatives describe as "anti-Russian hysteria".

State-level governments hold significant powers over areas including local education, policing and culture, while their delegates sit in the federal government's second chamber – the Bundesrat.

An AfD government in Saxony-Anhalt would be able to implement changes locally and gain a louder voice on the national stage.

The party remains strongest in the former communist east Germany but it is also leading the polls nationwide.

That is despite warnings that it has morphed from a Eurosceptic party, founded in 2013, into one that flirts with, or attracts, extremist support.

At one AfD rally, we saw a man wearing a T-shirt that read Arisch - the German word for Aryan that the Nazis used to promote their false theories of a master race.

We do not know whether the man was a party supporter, a member or merely an attendee. He would not talk to us.

Saxony-Anhalt is one of several states where the party is officially classed as right-wing extremist.

Domestic intelligence charges the local branch with being infused by a "racist ideology" and anti-constitutional aims.

The AfD, which says it is a conservative, libertarian movement, dismisses these designations as politicised smears and rejects any comparisons with National Socialism.

Ulrich Siegmund has not ruled out getting rid of domestic intelligence (BfV) in the state if the AfD wins a majority.

Other parties won't go into coalition with the AfD, as part of what is known as the Brandmauer or firewall that keeps the far right from government.

That is why it must seek a parliamentary majority in order to be sure of securing power.

In Saxony-Anhalt, it is no longer about creating cracks in the firewall but rather trying to bypass it altogether.

Pulling that off will likely depend on whether other, smaller parties get enough votes in order to pass a 5% threshold that allows them to enter parliament.

Politics is maths and Germany is no different, even if the maths can be quite convoluted.

But if the AfD does score a decisive victory, then a party that uses anti-establishment rhetoric to grow its support will face a test it has never faced before.

Grievances could still be laid at the door of the federal government in Berlin, but the AfD would no longer solely be able to rail against those in office because it would be in office itself.

Saxony-Anhalt may be a relatively small state, by population, but it is about to host one hell of an election.

articles.title: Tunisia arrests journalist Mohamed Yousfi amid crackdown on critics
articles.summary: Tunisia faces criticism as prosecutions of journalists continue under President Kais Saied’s rule.
articles.body:
Tunisian police have arrested prominent journalist Mohamed Yousfi, a vocal critic of President Kais Saied’s rule, the head of the National Syndicate of Tunisian Journalists told Reuters.

According to local journalists, police said that Yousfi, the editor-in-chief of the investigative news website Al-Qatiba, was brought in on Friday for questioning. The focus of the investigation is unknown.

Tunisian authorities have not yet commented on the arrest, which is the latest in a string of prosecutions of media figures and activists in Tunisia this year.

Khaoula Boukrim, founder of the news website TUMEDIA, who fled to France last year, was sentenced in June to four years in absentia.

Prominent journalist Zied el-Heni was sentenced in May to one year in prison, while broadcaster Mourad Zeghidi and political commentator Borhen Bsaies were sentenced in January to three and a half years.

Rights groups have warned of a widening crackdown on independent voices in Tunisia under Saied, whose rule has dismantled democratic safeguards, enabling authorities to pursue journalists and critics more aggressively.

On Thursday, Tunisia’s Court of Cassation upheld a mass trial against 40 figures, including opposition leaders, lawyers and human rights defenders convicted of conspiring to overthrow Saied.

“The ruling confirms that the judiciary is not independent,” said Haifa Chebbi, a lawyer whose father, opposition leader Najib Chebbi, was among those sentenced to 12 years.

Tunisia’s Minister of Justice Leila Jaffel said the defendants sought to destabilise the country.
